cards.heading: The latency ladder everyone should memorize
cards.hook: Memory read is ~100ns, an SSD random read is ~150μs, a disk seek is ~10ms, and a cross-country network round trip is ~50ms.
cards.body: Five orders of magnitude apart, and knowing where you sit on this ladder is most of system design intuition.

cards.heading: Storage math starts with one formula
cards.hook: Total Storage = Data Size per Record × Number of Records × Replication Factor — almost every capacity estimate reduces to this one line.

cards.heading: The 80/20 rule for traffic
cards.hook: 80% of traffic happens in 20% of the day, which is why peak bandwidth is usually estimated at about 4x the daily average, not the average itself.

cards.heading: Design for 10x, not 2x
cards.hook: The standard rule of thumb is to size a system for ten times current load, not a comfortable 2-3x margin.
cards.body: Growth that outpaces a small buffer arrives faster than most re-architecture projects can be finished.

cards.heading: Replication always costs 3x
cards.hook: A typical distributed system replicates data three times for fault tolerance, so your real storage bill is your raw estimate times three — before a single index is added.

cards.heading: Compression ratios vary wildly by data type
cards.hook: Text and JSON compress 2-5x and logs compress 3-10x, but images are already compressed and barely shrink further.
cards.body: Assuming a flat compression ratio across every data type is a common estimation mistake.

cards.heading: A well-cached system hits 80-95% of the time
cards.hook: An 80-95% cache hit rate is the standard baseline for a well-designed cache layer.
cards.body: Anything meaningfully below that usually means the cache key or TTL strategy needs rethinking, not more memory.

cards.heading: Index overhead adds 20-50% to a table's real size
cards.hook: Database Size = Records × Avg Record Size × Index Overhead, and that overhead routinely runs 20-50% on top of the raw data.
cards.body: A capacity estimate that forgets indexes is routinely off by half.

cards.heading: The order of magnitude is the point
cards.hook: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is about the right order of magnitude, not an exact number.
cards.body: Round liberally, and focus on whether a design is built for millions or billions, not whether it's 1.2 or 1.4 of something.

cards.heading: A billion users' profiles is smaller than you'd think
cards.hook: A billion user profiles at roughly 1KB each is about 1TB of raw data — with 3x replication, that's 3TB, which fits on a handful of modern database servers.

cards.heading: CDN is the answer to download bandwidth, not origin scaling
cards.hook: A video service's 50 Tbps of concurrent viewer bandwidth collapses to about 5 Tbps once a CDN absorbs the traffic.
cards.body: The origin servers were never meant to serve that number directly.

cards.heading: Peak RPS is rarely the average
cards.hook: Requests per Second = Daily Requests / 86,400 is the average — multiply by 3-5x for the peak hour, which is the number that actually sizes your servers.

cards.heading: Forgetting the replication factor is the most common mistake
cards.hook: The single most common capacity-estimation mistake is forgetting to multiply by the replication factor.
cards.body: A storage number that looks fine at 1x quietly triples in production.

cards.heading: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read
cards.hook: Pre-computing a feed on every post write makes reads instant, but it explodes for a celebrity with millions of followers.
cards.body: Computing the feed on read instead avoids that write storm, at the cost of a slower feed load.

cards.heading: The hybrid feed strategy most systems actually use
cards.hook: Pre-compute feeds for accounts under about 1,000 followers and generate on-demand for everyone past that.
cards.body: It's the practical middle ground between fan-out-on-write and fan-out-on-read.

cards.heading: Celebrity accounts create hot partitions
cards.hook: A single celebrity account with millions of followers can overwhelm a feed fan-out system on its own.
cards.body: The fix is routing just those accounts to on-demand generation and aggressive caching instead of the normal write path.

cards.heading: Feed ranking isn't just recency
cards.hook: A typical feed ranks posts by a weighted blend: roughly 70% recency, 20% engagement, and 10% relationship strength with the poster.
cards.body: Not a strict reverse-chronological feed, even when it looks like one.

cards.heading: Media upload triggers a processing pipeline
cards.hook: An uploaded photo fans out into a thumbnail, a medium size, a large size, and any requested filter, all before the post is considered ready.

cards.heading: Layered cache TTLs match how fast data actually changes
cards.hook: User profiles cache for 24 hours, post metadata for 1 hour, and a feed for just 5 minutes.
cards.body: The TTL isn't arbitrary — it tracks how stale each kind of data is allowed to get.

cards.heading: Sharding by user_id keeps a user's own data together
cards.hook: Posts, profile, and relationships for one user land on the same shard where possible.
cards.body: That's what keeps a single profile page load from fanning out across the whole cluster.

cards.heading: Read-heavy by a factor of 100
cards.hook: A typical social feed sees roughly a 100:1 read-to-write ratio.
cards.body: That number is what justifies spending so much engineering effort on caching reads instead of optimizing the write path.

cards.heading: Full text search needs its own engine
cards.hook: Searching usernames, hashtags, and captions isn't a database query — it's routed to Elasticsearch with its own index.
cards.body: Fuzzy matching and geospatial search don't fit a relational WHERE clause.

cards.heading: Graceful degradation beats a cache outage taking down the app
cards.hook: When the cache layer fails, the system falls back to serving straight from the database instead of erroring out.
cards.body: Slower, but still working — which is the whole point of a cache being an optimization, not a dependency.

cards.heading: Stories trade retention for write volume
cards.hook: 24-hour story content gets a completely separate storage path from permanent posts — high write rate, but auto-deleted after a day.
cards.body: It never needs the same long-term replication and retention budget as a regular post.

cards.heading: Multiple data centers eliminate the single point of failure
cards.hook: No individual server, database replica, or even entire data center is allowed to be a single point of failure.
cards.body: Multi-region deployment with automatic traffic routing is what makes a regional outage invisible to users.

cards.heading: The load balancing algorithm depends on what's being balanced
cards.hook: Stateless API servers use least-connections, but sessions needing affinity use IP hash instead.
cards.body: The 'best' algorithm depends on whether the backend actually needs to remember you.

cards.heading: Counter-based generation beats hashing for short URLs
cards.hook: A hash of the long URL can collide and isn't guaranteed unique — an auto-incrementing counter encoded in Base62 guarantees uniqueness with zero collision handling.
cards.body: The cost is one database lookup per generation instead of none.

cards.heading: Base62 is just URL-safe compact counting
cards.hook: Base62 uses 0-9, a-z, and A-Z — 62 characters, chosen specifically because every one is URL-safe.
cards.body: Six characters of it already cover 56.8 billion unique codes.

cards.heading: 301 vs 302 is a real trade-off, not a technicality
cards.hook: A 301 redirect gets cached by the browser and is faster on repeat visits, but the server stops seeing repeat clicks to track.
cards.body: A 302 is slower per click but gives full analytics on every single one.

cards.heading: Cache warming preloads what you already know is hot
cards.hook: Rather than waiting for the cache to fill up organically, the top 1,000 most-accessed short URLs get loaded in proactively on startup, with a longer TTL than everything else.

cards.heading: LRU eviction with a longer TTL for hot keys
cards.hook: Normal URLs get a 1-hour cache TTL, but URLs identified as high-traffic get bumped to 24 hours.
cards.body: The eviction policy isn't uniform — it's weighted toward what's actually getting hit.

cards.heading: Click tracking happens async, off the redirect's critical path
cards.hook: The redirect response doesn't wait for the click to be logged — the event is published to a queue and processed separately.
cards.body: Tracking never adds latency to the thing the user is actually waiting for.

cards.heading: Malicious URL checks run through a dedicated safety API
cards.hook: Before a long URL is ever shortened, it gets checked against a phishing/malware blacklist service like Google Safe Browsing.
cards.body: The shortening service doesn't try to detect malware itself.

cards.heading: Rate limiting with Redis is a two-command pattern
cards.hook: INCR a per-user counter key, and the first time it's created, set an EXPIRE on it.
cards.body: That's the entire implementation of a rate limiter — no separate cron job needed to reset counts.
cards.code:
const current = await redis.incr(`ratelimit:${userId}`);
if (current === 1) await redis.expire(key, window);

cards.heading: Distributed ID generation avoids a single counter bottleneck
cards.hook: A single auto-increment counter becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure at scale.
cards.body: The standard fix is a distributed ID generator like Twitter's Snowflake, which hands out unique IDs without any one server owning the sequence.

cards.heading: Analytics flow through a stream, not a direct database write
cards.hook: A click event goes API server to Kafka topic to an analytics service to a time-series database.
cards.body: That decouples the hot redirect path from the slower job of aggregating click analytics.

cards.heading: Random strings need a uniqueness check hashing avoids
cards.hook: Generating a random short code is simple, but without a counter or hash guaranteeing uniqueness, you need a database check-and-retry loop.
cards.body: Collision probability only grows as more codes get used.

cards.heading: A control plane and a data plane are different layers
cards.hook: The API Gateway, instance management, and orchestration services form the control plane that decides what should happen.
cards.body: The hypervisor hosts actually running your VM are the data plane that makes it happen.

cards.heading: Instance placement is its own algorithm
cards.hook: Launching an instance isn't just 'start a VM' — it's checking availability-zone capacity, finding a suitable host, verifying resource room, honoring placement constraints, and only then reserving the resources.

cards.heading: An instance's lifecycle is a strict state machine
cards.hook: pending to running to stopping to stopped, or running straight to shutting-down to terminated.
cards.body: EC2 instances can't skip states, which is what makes their lifecycle predictable to automate against.

cards.heading: Hypervisors isolate tenants on the same physical hardware
cards.hook: CPU pinning, memory ballooning, and I/O throttling are what let multiple customers' instances share one physical host without one noisy neighbor starving another.

cards.heading: Launching an instance is an asynchronous, event-driven flow
cards.hook: A launch request doesn't block until the VM boots — it's recorded as pending, published as an event, picked up for placement, then handed to the hypervisor layer.
cards.body: Each step notifies the next instead of one long synchronous call.

cards.heading: Images and volumes are decoupled from compute
cards.hook: An AMI lives in object storage with its own metadata and versioning, entirely separate from any running instance.
cards.body: That's what lets the same image launch onto thousands of different instances in parallel.

cards.heading: A metadata database and a time-series database serve different jobs
cards.hook: Instance configuration lives in a relational metadata store, but the constant stream of CPU/memory/network metrics goes to a time-series database built for exactly that write pattern.

cards.heading: Sequential IDs leak information a production system shouldn't expose
cards.hook: An instance ID that's sequential reveals how many instances exist and in what order they were created.
cards.body: Production systems generate opaque, non-sequential identifiers instead.

cards.heading: Rate limiting lives at the API Gateway, not buried in each service
cards.hook: Authentication, routing, and rate limiting all happen once at the API Gateway layer.
cards.body: Every service behind it inherits that protection without reimplementing it.

cards.heading: Health checks distinguish system failure from instance failure
cards.hook: A system status check verifies the underlying hypervisor host is healthy, while a separate instance status check verifies the specific VM is reachable.
cards.body: The two can fail independently and point to very different fixes.

cards.heading: Matching riders to drivers is a ranked, timed negotiation
cards.hook: The matching service filters by availability, rating, and ride-type, ranks by proximity and ETA, then gives the chosen driver a 30-second window to accept before moving to the next candidate.

cards.heading: Geohashing turns location into a fast lookup
cards.hook: Converting latitude/longitude into a geohash turns 'find nearby drivers' into a sorted-set range query instead of scanning every driver's coordinates one by one.

cards.heading: Redis Geo commands do spatial queries out of the box
cards.hook: GEOADD stores a driver's coordinates and GEORADIUS finds everyone within a given radius, sorted by distance.
cards.body: Uber's 'nearby drivers' problem fits directly into a Redis data structure built for it.
cards.code:
redis.geoadd('drivers:locations', lng, lat, driverId);
redis.georadius('drivers:locations', lng, lat, 2, 'km');

cards.heading: Surge pricing is a live demand-to-supply ratio, zone by zone
cards.hook: A city is divided into geohash grid zones, and each zone's ride requests in the last 5 minutes divided by its available drivers maps directly to a surge multiplier, capped around 2.5x.

cards.heading: Location updates are throttled, not blasted constantly
cards.hook: An active ride reports location every second, an available driver every 5 seconds, and an idle driver only every 30.
cards.body: Update frequency scales down with how much that location actually matters right now.

cards.heading: Write-behind caching for high-frequency, low-durability-need data
cards.hook: Driver location updates go straight to Redis and only get written to the time-series database asynchronously afterward.
cards.body: Durability can lag by seconds for data that's obsolete within seconds anyway.

cards.heading: Sharding by city avoids most cross-shard queries entirely
cards.hook: Riders, drivers, and rides are partitioned by city or region, since almost every query is already naturally scoped to one city.

cards.heading: Payment never touches the raw card number
cards.hook: Full credit card numbers are never stored — payment tokens from the gateway stand in for them.
cards.body: The actual charge happens through a PCI-compliant processor, not in-house.

cards.heading: Notifications go through a queue, not a direct call
cards.hook: Ride-matched, driver-arriving, and payment-processed events all flow through Kafka to notification workers.
cards.body: A slow push-notification provider never blocks the ride flow itself.

cards.heading: A fare is base plus distance plus time, times surge
cards.hook: Base Fare + (Distance × Rate) + (Time × Rate), multiplied by whatever the current surge multiplier is for that zone.
cards.body: Four numbers combine into every fare shown to a rider.

cards.heading: WebSockets replace polling for anything real-time
cards.hook: A rider watching their driver approach isn't polling an endpoint every few seconds — it's a persistent WebSocket connection pushing updates the moment they happen.

cards.heading: Cross-city rides are the exception that breaks city-sharding
cards.hook: Sharding by city works until a rider travels to a different city mid-trip or books a ride there.
cards.body: Handled either by replicating user data across relevant shards or keeping a small global user table as an escape hatch.

cards.heading: Active-active data centers, not just a hot standby
cards.hook: High availability here means multiple data centers actually serving traffic simultaneously, with automatic failover and cross-region replication.
cards.body: Not a single primary with an idle backup waiting to be promoted.

cards.heading: Email delivery goes through an abstraction over multiple providers
cards.hook: SES, SendGrid, and Mailgun all sit behind one delivery service.
cards.body: If one provider's reputation or uptime degrades, traffic shifts to another without the rest of the system noticing.

cards.heading: Retry logic has to tell transient failures from permanent ones
cards.hook: A rate-limit or transient error gets retried with exponential backoff, but a permanent failure gets marked as bounced immediately and never retried.
cards.body: Retrying a hard bounce just wastes attempts and hurts sender reputation.

cards.heading: Provider load balancing isn't just round-robin
cards.hook: Email providers can be chosen round-robin, by weighted capacity, by current least load, or by strict priority with fallback.
cards.body: The right strategy depends on whether you're optimizing for cost, reliability, or both.

cards.heading: Rendered templates get cached per audience segment
cards.hook: Instead of re-rendering the same template for every recipient, a rendered version is cached per contact segment and reused.
cards.body: Invalidated only when the template or that segment's data changes.

cards.heading: A/B test winners are picked by statistical significance
cards.hook: Each variant's open/click/conversion rate gets compared with a chi-square or t-test at 95% confidence.
cards.body: Only a statistically significant winner gets sent to the remaining audience — not a gut call on whichever number looks bigger.

cards.heading: Open tracking is a 1x1 invisible pixel
cards.hook: A transparent 1-pixel image, loaded from a unique tracking URL per recipient, is still the standard way email opens get measured.
cards.body: No open event without that pixel request landing.

cards.heading: Click tracking rewrites every link in the email
cards.hook: Every link gets swapped for a tracking URL encoding the campaign, recipient, and original destination, which logs the click and then redirects.

cards.heading: Delivery is queued, not sent inline with the API request
cards.hook: Creating a campaign doesn't send a single email synchronously — rendered emails go onto a delivery queue, processed by workers.
cards.body: That's what lets millions of sends happen without the triggering API call blocking.

cards.heading: Real-time and batch analytics serve different needs
cards.hook: Tracking events update live campaign stats in real time, while a separate batch job aggregates the same events hourly or daily for deeper reporting.
cards.body: One pipeline, two different latency requirements.

cards.heading: Templates support variables and conditionals, not just substitution
cards.hook: A template isn't just {{contact.first_name}} swapped in — it supports conditionals like showing a VIP section only for tagged contacts.
cards.body: That's what makes one template serve many different audiences.

cards.heading: Bounce handling protects sender reputation, not just one email
cards.hook: A permanent bounce gets marked immediately so the system stops retrying.
cards.body: Repeatedly hitting a dead address is exactly what gets a sending domain's reputation flagged by every major inbox provider.

cards.heading: Eventual consistency for analytics is an accepted trade-off
cards.hook: Campaign open/click counts don't need to be strongly consistent the instant an event happens.
cards.body: That's an explicit trade-off in exchange for never slowing down the actual send pipeline.

cards.heading: Compliance isn't optional for a mass-email system
cards.hook: Unsubscribe handling, CAN-SPAM/GDPR compliance, and suppression lists aren't an afterthought bolted onto an email platform.
cards.body: Sending to someone who opted out is a legal problem, not just a UX one.

cards.heading: A distributed lock stops the same cron job running twice
cards.hook: Before processing scheduled reminders, the job acquires a Redis lock with a timeout — if another instance is already running, this one just exits instead of double-sending.

cards.heading: Smart scheduling sends reminders when a customer actually reads email
cards.hook: The system looks at a customer's historical open times and schedules their next reminder for whenever they're statistically most likely to be reading email.
cards.body: It defaults to 10 AM local time only when there's no history yet.

cards.heading: Multi-channel fallback: email, SMS, WhatsApp in sequence
cards.hook: A single reminder can fan out across multiple channels, and failure on one doesn't block the others.
cards.body: A WhatsApp failure still lets the email and SMS attempts go through independently.

cards.heading: Reconciliation is a confidence-scored waterfall, not one rule
cards.hook: An incoming payment is matched by exact invoice-number reference first, then amount-plus-fuzzy-name, then amount-plus-date-proximity, then a trained ML model.
cards.body: Each tier produces a confidence score, and only high-confidence matches auto-reconcile.

cards.heading: Confidence thresholds decide automation vs. a human in the loop
cards.hook: Above 95% confidence, a payment auto-reconciles with no human involved. Between 70 and 95%, a human sees suggested matches. Below 70%, it's flagged for manual review.
cards.body: The system automates exactly as much as it can trust itself to.

cards.heading: Email sending can be the biggest line item in your cloud bill
cards.hook: At scale, sending 60 million emails a month costs roughly $720K a year — more than the compute, more than the primary database.
cards.body: 'Just send an email' isn't free once volume gets real.

cards.heading: 7-year audit log retention dwarfs the actual invoice data
cards.hook: 100 million invoices are about 1TB of data, but 7 years of compliance-driven audit logs come out to roughly 1.3 petabytes.
cards.body: The audit trail, not the business data, is what actually drives the storage bill.

cards.heading: A payment link gets UTM parameters baked in automatically
cards.hook: Every reminder's payment link is generated with UTM tracking parameters already attached.
cards.body: That's how ops can see exactly which reminder channel and campaign actually drove the payment.

cards.heading: Old processed records get cleaned up automatically
cards.hook: Reminders that are sent, cancelled, or failed get deleted after 90 days.
cards.body: The system actively prunes its own operational history instead of letting a table grow forever.

cards.heading: OAuth2 is the standard pattern for third-party accounting tools
cards.hook: Connecting QuickBooks isn't a direct API key exchange — it's a full OAuth2 redirect flow.
cards.body: The integration needs ongoing, revocable access to someone else's accounting data, not a one-time pull.

cards.heading: A paused invoice stops the follow-up engine cold
cards.hook: A single followup_paused flag checked on every reminder cycle is enough to stop all future automated contact for that invoice.
cards.body: Critical for when a customer disputes a charge and the last thing you want is an automated reminder firing anyway.

cards.heading: Cost estimates reveal where the real scaling pressure is
cards.hook: Database and storage costs each land in the low hundreds of thousands per year, but per-unit costs like email sending scale linearly with usage in a way flat infrastructure costs don't.

cards.heading: Sync jobs run on their own cadence
cards.hook: Integration syncs with tools like QuickBooks run every 15 minutes via their own scheduled job.
cards.body: Completely decoupled from whatever a user happens to be doing in the dashboard at that moment.

cards.heading: A reconciliation dashboard exists because automation won't catch everything
cards.hook: However good the automatic matching gets, a drag-and-drop dashboard for manual reconciliation is still a first-class part of the design.
cards.body: The system is built assuming it will sometimes be wrong, not hoping it never is.

cards.heading: Refresh token rotation turns theft into an alarm
cards.hook: Every refresh token is single-use — using it issues a new one and marks the old one spent.
cards.body: If that same old token is ever used again, it's proof of theft, and every session for that user gets revoked immediately.

cards.heading: JWKS caching keeps token verification off the network
cards.hook: Verifying an access token's signature happens against a locally cached public key, refreshed only when an unrecognized key ID shows up.
cards.body: Validation under peak load never makes a live call to the signing service.

cards.heading: Key rotation doesn't invalidate tokens already in flight
cards.hook: A new signing key gets published alongside the old one, both valid at once.
cards.body: New tokens sign with the new key, old tokens keep validating until they naturally expire, and only then is the old key removed.

cards.heading: Logout everywhere means walking every active session
cards.hook: Forcing a logout across all devices means iterating every session for that user, deleting each refresh token, and revoking each still-valid access token's ID.
cards.body: There's no single switch that invalidates a user's tokens globally.

cards.heading: One stateful check survives on an otherwise stateless hot path
cards.hook: Token validation is local and fast, but one Redis lookup against a revocation list still happens on every request.
cards.body: Logout everywhere and breach response have to actually work, and a purely stateless design can't support either.

cards.heading: MFA policy is tenant-configurable, not a platform constant
cards.hook: Whether to trust an enterprise customer's own IdP-asserted MFA or always challenge again is a per-tenant setting.
cards.body: Enterprise buyers negotiate their own security posture into contracts, so this can't be hardcoded.

cards.heading: JIT provisioning creates the user on their first SSO login
cards.hook: A user doesn't need to exist in the system beforehand to log in via SSO — their first successful assertion creates their internal account on the spot.

cards.heading: Claims embedded in the JWT skip a network call on every request
cards.hook: Roles and permissions are embedded directly in the signed token, so most authorization checks never call the Authorization Service at all.
cards.body: Only less-common, resource-specific checks make that extra hop.

cards.heading: Accepting staleness is the trade-off for skipping that network call
cards.hook: Embedding roles in the JWT means a permission change can take up to one token's lifetime to actually take effect.
cards.body: An accepted trade-off — minutes of staleness against a network round-trip on every single request.

cards.heading: GDPR erasure pseudonymizes the audit trail instead of deleting it
cards.hook: Deleting a user's profile is straightforward, but their audit log entries get pseudonymized — subject replaced with a stable non-reversible token — rather than removed outright.
cards.body: Compliance retention law requires keeping the trail intact.

cards.heading: Password hashing is deliberately slow, and kept off the main thread
cards.hook: Argon2id is tuned to take about 250ms per hash on purpose — slow enough to make brute-forcing expensive.
cards.body: It runs in a worker thread pool specifically so that cost never blocks the event loop handling other requests.

cards.heading: SMS is the weakest MFA factor, treated accordingly
cards.hook: SMS-based MFA is kept as a fallback, not a primary option, and rate-limited more aggressively than TOTP or WebAuthn.
cards.body: It's the MFA method most abused by SIM-swapping attacks.

cards.heading: A degraded authorization service fails open to the last known claims
cards.hook: If the Authorization Service goes down, downstream services keep trusting the roles already embedded in a verified token rather than rejecting every request.
cards.body: A platform-wide outage would be a worse failure than minutes of stale permissions.

cards.heading: One tenant's broken SSO doesn't touch any other tenant
cards.hook: If a specific enterprise customer's identity provider goes down, only that tenant's SSO logins are affected.
cards.body: Password login and every other tenant's sessions keep working completely unaffected.

cards.heading: Audit writes are guaranteed, but never block the response
cards.hook: A login response doesn't wait for its audit log entry to finish writing.
cards.body: That write is still guaranteed to happen via an async, durable pipeline — not just a best-effort fire-and-forget log line.

cards.heading: Signing keys never leave the KMS, even to the application
cards.hook: The Token Service asks KMS to sign things — the actual private signing key is never exported into application config or memory where a compromised server could leak it.

cards.heading: The access/refresh token split exists because one token can't do both jobs
cards.hook: A single JWT could work for everything, but then it couldn't be revoked without an extra lookup anyway.
cards.body: Splitting into a stateless, short-lived access token plus a revocable, opaque refresh token gets speed AND revocability instead of picking one.

cards.heading: Per-tenant SSO federation is a sales requirement, not a nice-to-have
cards.hook: Enterprise buyers won't migrate their entire workforce identity onto a vendor's login system.
cards.body: Supporting each tenant's own SAML/OIDC identity provider is what actually closes enterprise deals, not a technical preference.
